s: Part six.
Claude Code in pipelines.

By the end of this part, you'll know how to run Claude Code with nobody watching, how to gate a merge on something a machine can read, how to stop duplicate and biased reviews, and how to control what a pipeline run inherits.
Plain version.
Leaving a voicemail that ends with a question is pointless if nobody will ever listen and call back.
The conversation just stalls.
A pipeline is a room with nobody in it.
Whatever runs there must say everything up front.
It must expect no reply.
And it must bring its own configuration, rather than trusting whatever happens to be lying around on the machine.
The technical name for that room is continuous integration and continuous delivery, usually said as C-I-C-D.
It's the automated system, such as GitHub Actions or GitLab, that builds, tests and checks code on a server every time someone pushes.
The episode on this topic opens with exactly our first question.
Question one.
Practice question D3-020.
Here's the scenario.
A GitHub Actions step runs claude, followed by a prompt asking it to review the failing tests and suggest fixes.
On a developer's laptop, it works, because the developer answers Claude's follow-up questions.
In the pipeline, the job sits idle until the workflow timeout kills it.
What's missing?
Take a second.
The answer.
Invoke it as claude -p, followed by the prompt.
The episode's presenter explains it well.
Locally, there's a human in the loop.
In the pipeline, Claude asks a clarifying question.
Nobody responds.
The job hangs.
And engineers blame the integration, when nothing is wrong with it except a missing flag.
In exam terms.
The -p flag, whose long form is --print, is the non-interactive mode.
One prompt in.
One response out.
A clean exit.
It reads standard input, so you can pipe a diff or a build log into it.
And it exits with zero on success, and non-zero on failure.
So later pipeline steps can branch on the result.
Now the wrong turns.
They're fabricated flags, and the presenter called them out as exam tricks.
Wrong: a --ci-mode flag.
Wrong: a --batch flag.
Wrong: a --headless flag.
Wrong: an environment variable called CLAUDE_HEADLESS.
Why?
None of them exist.
The -p flag is the single valid way to run Claude Code headless.
Hold on to this line.
In a pipeline, always -p.
Anything that sounds like headless mode or CI mode is invented.
Question two.
Practice question D3-021.
Here's the scenario.
A pipeline runs a Claude review with -p.
A later step blocks the merge if any finding is critical.
That step searches the prose output for the word critical.
It has blocked clean pull requests.
And it has passed a real critical bug that Claude described as severe.
The merge check must decide on a field the pipeline controls, not on phrasing.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Add --output-format json.
Add --json-schema, with a schema whose severity field only allows a fixed list of values, such as critical, major and minor.
Then gate the step with jq -e.
Plain version.
A form with a tick box marked critical, yes or no, can be sorted by a machine.
A free-text note saying this looks pretty bad cannot.
The pipeline needs the tick box, not the note.
In exam terms.
JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation, is a structured data format machines can parse.
With a schema supplied, the conforming output lands in a field called structured_output, in the result.
Then you gate the step with a command-line JSON tool called jq, run as jq -e.
That makes the step fail based on a parsed value.
The model's wording is never consulted.
As the presenter put it, default prose is great for humans, and useless for pipelines.
And the --output-format flag takes three values: text, json, or stream-json.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: tell Claude to end every response with a verdict line, and search for that line.
Why?
It's better than free prose.
But the gate still depends on the model's phrasing, rather than a field the pipeline owns.
Wrong: search for a maintained list of synonyms.
Why?
It's still pattern-matching on prose.
Still false blocks, and false passes.
Wrong: submit the review through the Message Batches API, because it returns structured results.
Why?
Batches have a twenty-four-hour processing window, and no latency guarantee.
So they're wrong for any blocking check.
The episode names that one directly: never use batches for a blocking pre-merge check.
One cross-reference for Domain four.
The --output-format flag shapes the command-line tool's wrapper document.
That's different from the API's structured output parameter.
That chapter disambiguates all the similar names.
Hold on to this line.
Gate a pipeline on a schema field checked by code.
Never on words in prose.
Question three.
Practice question D3-022.
The presenter flagged this one as a certain exam scenario.
How do you stop Claude doing double work?
Here's the scenario.
A pull request review job runs -p on every push.
Each small follow-up commit triggers a full re-review.
And Claude reposts the same comments it made on earlier pushes.
Developers have started muting the bot.
The runners are ephemeral containers, meaning each job gets a fresh machine that is thrown away afterwards.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
In a prior step, fetch Claude's earlier comments on the pull request, using gh, the GitHub command-line tool.
Save them to a file.
Pass them into the fresh -p session.
And ask only for net-new issues.
Plain version.
A new proofreader who hasn't seen your earlier notes will circle the same typos again.
Hand them the list of what's already been flagged, and ask them to mark only what's new.
In exam terms, the episode calls this the deduplication loop.
Fetch the previous comments.
Pass them into fresh session context.
Generate new comments only.
Repeat.
It keeps the fresh session's objectivity, while ending notification fatigue.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: use claude -c -p to continue the previous session, so Claude remembers.
Why?
Continuing depends on conversation state that an ephemeral runner does not keep.
And a same-session reviewer tends to rationalize its earlier reasoning.
Wrong: review only the first push to each pull request.
Why?
It removes duplicates by never reviewing the new code.
Wrong: report only critical findings.
Why?
It hides legitimate issues.
And it still re-reports the same critical ones every push.
Hold on to this line.
Deduplicate by handing prior findings to a fresh session.
Not by continuing an old one.
That leads straight to the next one, and the idea the presenter called the psychology of review.
Question four.
Practice question D3-024.
Here's the scenario.
A pipeline job uses -p to generate unit tests for changed code.
Then it continues the same session with claude -c -p, to review those tests.
The review almost never flags anything.
Yet the tests routinely miss negative paths.
Those are the cases where input is bad, or something fails.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Run the review as a separate job, in a fresh -p session, with test standards supplied by the project CLAUDE.md.
Plain version.
Asking the author of an essay to proofread it straight away rarely finds much, because they read what they meant to write.
A colleague who didn't write it sees what's actually on the page.
The presenter's version was developers and testers.
The developer tests along the path they built.
The tester, with fresh eyes, thinks of new scenarios.
In exam terms.
A session that wrote the code retains the reasoning behind it, and tends to review by rationalizing.
A fresh session has nothing to defend.
And because a fresh session remembers nothing, CLAUDE.md is how shared standards reach every job.
Coding standards.
Review criteria.
Security policies.
Testing requirements, like naming patterns, mocking rules, and coverage targets.
Every new session loads it automatically.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: keep the continued session, but instruct Claude to be highly critical and list at least three weaknesses.
Why?
The bias remains.
And a quota invites invented findings.
Wrong: increase --max-turns.
Why?
That's just more time for a biased reviewer.
Wrong: add JSON output.
Why?
It helps gating, but it doesn't change the review's quality.
Now a contrast segment on sessions, since this spans chapters.
Continuing a session keeps the reasoning.
That's useful for picking up your own work, and harmful for reviewing it.
A fresh session gives objectivity.
The price is that it knows nothing.
So you pay that price back with CLAUDE.md for standing rules, and with explicit context, like prior findings, for anything situational.
You'll meet the same resume, fork, or fresh-start decision in the chapter on context management.
Hold on to this line.
Separate jobs, separate sessions, with CLAUDE.md carrying the standards into each one.
Question five.
Practice question D3-023.
This one is about controlling what the pipeline inherits.
And it's pick two.
Here's the scenario.
A conventions gate runs -p on a shared self-hosted runner.
Three requirements.
It must apply the repository's committed CLAUDE.md and rules.
It must not execute any hooks from engineers' personal settings on that machine.
And it should see the pull request diff, without being granted shell access.
Which two?
Take a second.
The answers.
First, --setting-sources project.
Second, compute the diff in an earlier step, pipe it into -p on standard input, and pre-approve only the read-only tools Read, Grep and Glob.
Plain version.
When you borrow a colleague's desk for the day, you want the company handbook on it.
But not their personal sticky notes telling you to do things their way.
And if all you need is one document, someone hands it to you.
You don't get the keys to the filing room.
In exam terms.
The --setting-sources flag takes a list drawn from user, project and local.
With just project, it loads the repository's configuration, while skipping user and local configuration.
So personal hooks stay out.
And piping the data removes any need for a shell permission.
That's least privilege.
Now the wrong turns.
The big one is --bare.
Wrong: --bare.
Why?
Bare mode skips automatic discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md itself.
MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is how external tools plug in.
Bare sounds perfect for keeping personal hooks out.
But it would also skip the committed CLAUDE.md that this gate exists to apply.
Bare suits jobs that must ignore everything the repository and the machine ship.
It also never reads stored login credentials.
So you must set the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY variable explicitly.
Two more wrong turns.
Wrong: --permission-mode plan, to stop user hooks.
Why?
Plan mode governs edits, not configuration discovery.
Wrong: pre-approving `Bash(git diff*)` through --allowedTools, with no space before the asterisk.
Why?
It grants shell access the job doesn't need.
And, as you heard in part two, it also matches commands like git diff-index.
So the contrast.
Bare, versus setting-sources project.
Bare drops everything auto-discovered, CLAUDE.md included.
You pass back only what you need, with explicit flags for settings, MCP configuration, or an appended system prompt.
So every input is visible in the workflow file.
Setting-sources project keeps the team's committed configuration, and drops the personal.
When does bare win?
An exam-style item in the notes shows it.
A nightly summary job on a shared runner starts reformatting files and opening commits.
That's after another team rebuilt the base image, with no change to the workflow.
Discovered hooks or skills on the new image explain it.
And bare restores predictable behavior.
The distractors there all treat symptoms.
Plan mode.
JSON output to detect edits afterwards.
Version pinning with verbose logging.
Hold on to this line.
Setting-sources project keeps the team's config and drops personal config.
Bare drops everything, CLAUDE.md included.
A few remaining pieces of this task statement.
First, the GitHub Action.
The higher-level GitHub option is the Claude Code GitHub Action.
To set it up, you run /install-github-app, or install the Claude GitHub App.
You add an API key or OAuth token secret.
And you copy a workflow file.
Its mode depends on one input: the prompt input.
With no prompt input, it runs in interactive mode.
It waits for someone to write @claude in an issue or pull request comment.
And it replies in a comment.
With a prompt input, it runs in automation mode, on any event, including a scheduled cron job.
And it writes results to the workflow run log.
So a mention-driven reviewer omits the prompt.
And a Monday dependency report supplies one.
It also checks the triggering actor.
Users need write access.
And bot accounts are rejected unless listed in the allowed_bots setting.
That stops two bots triggering each other in a loop.
For GitLab, the shape is the same.
One job in the pipeline file.
The API key as a masked variable.
The command-line tool installed in the setup script.
And claude -p with --permission-mode acceptEdits, when the job should open a merge request.
And the governing principle for all of it.
Pipelines are where permission design becomes the control.
Five habits.
One.
Grant least privilege, with precise tool rules.
Two.
Keep credentials in secrets.
Three.
Pipe data in, rather than granting tools to fetch it.
Four.
Fail steps on parsed signals.
Five.
Route every change through a pull or merge request.
The notes call the alternative the overprivileged pipeline.
A broad permission mode, because writing an allowlist felt tedious.
Plus whatever the runner image carries.
That's part six.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
A pipeline run must name everything it needs on the command line, and inherit nothing by accident.
Coming up next: the trap round.
The trap round.
Rapid fire.
For each one, the pattern is: if you see this, think that.
I'll take them in small groups, so you always know where you are.
First group.
Instruction files and scopes.
If you see a teammate or the pipeline not getting conventions that work for one person, think: check the config location.
Move it from the user file to the committed project file.
If you see CLAUDE.local.md offered as a way to share with the team, think: personal, and ignored by version control.
Never shared.
If you see project scope overrides user scope, or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md loads later and wins, think: scopes are additive.
Delete the contradiction.
If you see capitals, CRITICAL, MUST, or repeating a line to give it weight, think: emphasis is not precedence, and not enforcement.
If you see imports offered to cut startup tokens, think: imports organize, they do not economize.
If you see imports offered for conditional loading, think: no.
Imports expand at launch.
If you see a CLAUDE.md heading that says for files matching some path, think: CLAUDE.md has no path prefixes.
That heading is just text.
Next group.
What loads, and when.
If you see a file-type convention scattered across the tree, think: a rule in the rules folder, with paths.
If you see each package team wanting its own file beside its own code, think: a subfolder CLAUDE.md.
If you see a rule with no frontmatter causing cross-contamination and constant cost, think: add paths.
Without paths, it loads every session.
If you see a single-star glob missing nested files, think: double star, for any depth.
If you see brace-expansion budget offered as the cause for a pattern with no braces, think: it cannot apply.
If you see the question, what should they do first about a missing rule, think: run /memory after Claude reads the matching file.
If you see a path rule forgotten after a long session compacted, think: path rules are not re-injected.
They reload on the next matching read.
Now the one that cuts across everything.
If you see never, must hold every time, or guarantee, think: hook or permission rule.
Not prose.
Not managed policy.
Not plan mode.
Next group.
Skills.
If you see a side-effecting command that must never fire on its own, think: disable-model-invocation true.
If you see user-invocable false offered for that job, think: reversed.
That makes it Claude-only.
If you see argument-hint offered to validate or bind input, think: hints only. arguments binds named placeholders.
If you see allowed-tools described as blocking tools for the session, think: the notes say it pre-approves for one turn, and restricts nothing.
But if the question itself frames it as a restriction, answer in the question's terms.
If you see a team-wide or session-wide pre-approval, think: an allow rule in project permission settings.
Not skill frontmatter.
If you see a stale personal skill breaking one engineer's command, think: personal beats project on a name clash.
Delete or rename the personal skill.
If you see exploration flooding the main conversation, think: context: fork, with a body written as a task.
And background: false, if you need the answer this turn.
If you see context: fork on a skill that is only guidelines, think: fork-forgetting.
It returns nothing useful.
Next group.
Planning and refinement.
If you see a one-sentence, single-file fix under time pressure, think: direct execution, and show the test passing.
If you see unfamiliar code, several valid designs, many files, and a costly failure, think: plan mode, and edit the plan with Control G.
If you see plan mode offered as a safety guarantee, think: workflow control, not a security boundary.
Its blocks are not enforced where bypass permissions are available.
If you see Claude saying all tests pass with no output, think: verification by assertion.
Require evidence.
And for a guarantee, a Stop hook.
If you see two failed corrections on the same issue, think: clear the context, and write a better prompt with a failing test.
If you see raising the turn limit to fix a loop that is not converging, think: the loop lacks a signal, not a budget.
If you see fanning out across many files before the prompt works on a sample, think: refine sequentially first, then fan out.
If you see implementing in the same session as the interview, think: write the spec to a file, and start fresh.
Last group.
Pipelines.
If you see a pipeline job hanging until timeout, think: -p.
If you see --ci-mode, --batch, --headless, or CLAUDE_HEADLESS, think: fabricated.
If you see a merge gate searching prose for a word, think: --output-format json, --json-schema with an enum, and jq -e on structured_output.
If you see the Batches API for a blocking check, think: twenty-four-hour window, no latency guarantee.
Wrong tool.
If you see the same review comments reposted on every push, think: fetch prior comments, and pass them into a fresh session.
If you see claude -c -p to continue a session for review, think: rationalization.
And state an ephemeral runner does not keep.
And the last three, about what a runner inherits.
If you see personal hooks leaking into a job that must still apply CLAUDE.md, think: --setting-sources project.
Not --bare.
If you see a rebuilt runner image suddenly changing a job's behavior, think: --bare.
Plus an explicit ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
If you see a shell rule with no space before the asterisk, think: the grant is wider than intended.
And better still, pipe the data in.
That's the trap round.

Closing recap.
Ten things to remember.
For each one, you'll get the plain version first.
Then the technical name.
One.
Instruction files stack up.
They do not overrule each other.
When two contradict, delete one.
The technical name: CLAUDE.md scopes are additive.
Managed policy, user, project and local, concatenated from the root down.
Two.
Your personal file never leaves your machine.
So team rules go in the file the repository carries.
The technical name: user scope at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, versus a committed project CLAUDE.md.
And the gitignored CLAUDE.local.md, for personal project notes.
Three.
Splitting a big instruction file into pieces helps people own their parts.
But it saves nothing.
The technical name: at-path imports expand at launch, up to four hops.
They organize without economizing.
Four.
Conventions for one kind of file should appear only when that kind of file is touched.
The technical name: a rule in .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter globs.
One star is one level.
Two stars is any depth.
And a rule with no paths loads every session.
Five.
When something doesn't seem to be loading, check what actually loaded before changing anything.
The technical name: the /memory command, backed by /context, checked after Claude reads a matching file.
Six.
A reusable procedure belongs in a card pulled on demand, shared through the repository.
And anything with side effects should be startable only by a person.
The technical name: a project skill in .claude/skills/, with disable-model-invocation set to true. user-invocable false is the mirror.
And personal skills beat project skills on a name clash.
Seven.
A hint is not wiring.
And a one-time permission slip is not a lock.
The technical name: argument-hint is autocomplete, and arguments binds placeholders. allowed-tools pre-approves for the invoking turn, and restricts nothing.
Though the lesson deck calls it a restriction, so answer in a question's own terms.
Eight.
Send big investigations off to a helper with a clear task, so your main conversation stays clean.
The technical name: context: fork with an agent type, a body written as a self-contained task, and background: false to get the result in the same turn.
Nine.
Plan when being wrong is expensive.
Just do it when the change fits in one sentence.
And never mistake the planning habit for a lock.
The technical name: plan mode via Shift+Tab, /plan, or permissions.defaultMode set to plan.
Edited with Ctrl+G.
And not a security boundary where bypass permissions are available.
And refinement converges only on a signal Claude can read.

Ten.
In a pipeline, nobody is there to answer.
So the run must be one-shot, machine-readable, reviewed with fresh eyes, and carry its own settings.
The technical name: claude -p. --output-format json with --json-schema, gated by jq -e.
A fresh session per job, with prior findings passed in.
